questions.stem: Which statement about digital content is true?

options.text: Content found online is usually protected by copyright unless its license allows use
options.why: Correct. Being online does not make content free to use.

options.text: Anything posted online is in the public domain
options.why: Copyright still applies.
Code is intellectual property.

options.text: Only printed works can be copyrighted
options.why: Digital works can be too.

questions.explanation: Being online does not make content free to use.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best reason to include people with diverse backgrounds on a team designing an app?

options.text: They can identify needs and possible biases that a less diverse team might miss
options.why: Correct. Diverse perspectives improve computing innovations.

options.text: It guarantees the app will have no errors
options.why: No team composition guarantees that.

options.text: It makes the program run faster
options.why: Team makeup does not change run time.

options.text: It removes the need for user testing
options.why: Testing is still needed.

questions.explanation: Diverse perspectives improve computing innovations.

questions.stem: What is the decimal value of the binary number `00110101`?

options.why: Each 1 bit is worth its place value, not 1.
Correct. Add the place values of the 1 bits.
The places are 1, 2, 4, …, starting from the rightmost bit.
The rightmost bit is the 1s place, not the leftmost.

questions.stem: A social media platform built to help friends share photos is also used to spread false news quickly. This is an example of what?

options.why: That concerns access to technology.

options.text: An unintended harmful effect of a computing innovation
options.why: Correct. Creators did not plan this use.
That is a programming error.
That is unrelated.

questions.explanation: Creators did not plan this use.

questions.stem:

```text
result ← x MOD 6 * 5
DISPLAY (result)
```

What is displayed as a result of running the code segment?

options.why: MOD and * have equal precedence and are evaluated left to right.
MOD gives the remainder, not the quotient.

Recheck the remainder.

questions.stem: Ride-sharing apps let drivers earn money on flexible schedules but may reduce income for traditional taxi drivers. What does this show?

options.why: Decidability is unrelated.

options.text: The innovation has no harmful effects
options.why: Taxi drivers are harmed.

options.text: The innovation has only harmful effects
options.why: Drivers gain flexibility.

options.text: An effect can be beneficial for some people and harmful for others
options.why: Correct. Effects of innovations are rarely only good or only bad.

questions.explanation: Effects of innovations are rarely only good or only bad.

questions.stem: Which is the main benefit of procedural abstraction?

options.text: A procedure can be used by knowing what it does, without knowing how it works
options.why: Correct. That reduces complexity.

options.text: Procedures make programs run in parallel
options.why: Procedures do not create parallelism.
Variables are still needed.
Errors can still occur.

questions.explanation: That reduces complexity.

questions.stem: What is the probability that the expression `RANDOM(2, 11) ≥ 3` evaluates to true?

options.why: 3 itself is included by ≥.
Correct. The values 3 through 11 (9 of them) out of 10 equally likely values from 2 to 11.
RANDOM includes both 2 and 11, so there are 10 values.
That is the probability of the expression being false.

questions.explanation: RANDOM(2, 11) has 10 equally likely results; 9 of them are at least 3.

questions.stem: A user receives an email that looks like it is from their bank, asking them to click a link and enter their password. What is this attack called?

options.why: That is a fake wireless network.
Correct. Phishing tricks people into revealing information.
That is a numeric error.
That records keystrokes.

questions.explanation: Phishing tricks people into revealing information.

questions.stem: Why is multifactor authentication more secure than a password alone?

options.why: It protects logins, not against all malware.

options.text: An attacker who steals the password still needs another factor, such as a code on the user's phone
options.why: Correct. Multiple kinds of evidence are required.
A password is usually one of the factors.
That is not what multifactor means.

questions.explanation: Multiple kinds of evidence are required.

questions.stem: Which statement about lossless compression is true?

options.text: The original data can be completely restored
options.why: Correct. That is the defining property of lossless compression.
That describes lossy compression.

options.text: It always reduces a file to half its size
options.why: The reduction depends on the data.

options.text: It can only be used on text
options.why: It works on any data.

questions.explanation: That is the defining property of lossless compression.

questions.stem: A keyword is misspelled, so the program cannot be translated and run. Which type of error is this?

options.why: That would mean the value is larger than the fixed number of bits can represent.
That would mean the program runs, but the algorithm produces incorrect results.
That would mean the error occurs while the program is running and stops it.
Correct. The rules of the language are broken, so the program cannot run at all.

questions.explanation: The rules of the language are broken, so the program cannot run at all.

questions.stem: Machine learning finds patterns in medical data that help detect disease early, but the same data could reveal private health details. What does this illustrate?

options.text: Pattern finding is an undecidable problem
options.why: It is not.

options.text: Data analysis can have both beneficial and harmful effects
options.why: Correct. The same innovation can help and harm.
It can create privacy risks.

options.text: Medical data cannot be analyzed by computers
options.why: It can.

questions.explanation: The same innovation can help and harm.

questions.stem: Why were open protocols important to the growth of the Internet?

options.text: Any manufacturer can build devices that communicate with all others, letting the network scale
options.why: Correct. Open, shared rules allow anyone to connect.

options.text: They make each device a single point of failure
options.why: Openness does not cause that.

options.text: They limit the Internet to one company's devices
options.why: Open protocols do the opposite.
Protocols are not all about encryption.

questions.explanation: Open, shared rules allow anyone to connect.

questions.stem: Run-length encoding replaces each run of a repeated character with its count followed by the character, so AAAB becomes 3A1B. What is the encoding of `CCCCACCCCCAAAAAA`?

options.why: Each run is encoded separately, in order; runs are not merged.
The count comes before the character.
Correct. Each run is replaced by its length and character, in order.
Recount the first run.

questions.explanation: The runs are 4 C, 1 A, 5 C, 6 A, so the encoding is 4C1A5C6A. It is lossless: the original can be rebuilt exactly.

questions.stem: A survey collected only from people who use a particular app is used to describe the whole population. What is the main problem?

options.text: The sample may be biased, so the results may not represent everyone
options.why: Correct. Data collected from one group may not apply to others.

options.text: The data needs to be converted to binary first
options.why: All digital data is already binary.

options.text: The data set is too small to store
options.why: Size is not the issue.

options.text: Survey data cannot be analyzed by programs
options.why: It can be.

questions.explanation: Data collected from one group may not apply to others.

questions.stem: A simulation of a store's checkout lines assumes every customer takes exactly 2 minutes. What is the main limitation?

questions.stem: A company collects far more personal data than its app needs, which is legal in its country. Why might this still be a concern?

options.why: Some legal actions raise ethical issues.

options.text: Collecting unnecessary data can be unethical and increases privacy risks
options.why: Correct. Legal and ethical are not the same.

questions.stem: Which protocol is primarily responsible for addressing and routing packets to their destination?

options.why: Correct. IP handles addresses and routing.
TCP makes delivery reliable and ordered.
HTTP requests and sends web pages.
UDP sends data quickly without guarantees.

questions.stem: Which is an example of the digital divide?

questions.stem: What is open source software?

options.why: Correct. That is the definition of open source.

questions.stem: A coffee shop customer connects to a free network named after the shop, but it was set up by an attacker to capture traffic. What is this?

That is network reliability.
That is unrelated.

questions.explanation: A fake wireless network can intercept data.

questions.stem:
Consider the following code segment.

```text
x ← 3
total ← 0
REPEAT 7 TIMES
{
   x ← x + 1
   IF (x MOD 3 = 0)
   {
      total ← total + x
   }
}
DISPLAY (total)
```

What is displayed as a result of running the code segment?

options.why: Only values divisible by 3 are added.
Correct. x goes from 4 to 10; the multiples of 3 among them are added.
total adds the values, not 1 each time.
x is increased before the check in each pass.

questions.explanation: The values of x are 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10; the multiples of 3 add to 15.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of comments in program code?

options.why: Comments do not check the code.

options.text: To explain how the code works for people reading it, without affecting how it runs
options.why: Correct. Comments are documentation for programmers.

options.text: To encrypt the code so others cannot read it
options.why: Comments are plain text.

options.text: To make the program run faster
options.why: Comments do not change execution.

questions.explanation: Comments are documentation for programmers.

questions.stem: Two students work at one computer: one types the code while the other reviews each line and plans the next step, and they switch roles often. What is this practice called?

options.why: Correct. A driver and a navigator working together is pair programming.
That gathers input from many people online.
That runs operations at the same time on a computer.
That is public participation in research.

questions.explanation: A driver and a navigator working together is pair programming.

questions.stem: A program has 4 independent tasks that take 45, 34, 22, 42 seconds. The tasks can run in parallel on two processors, and each task runs entirely on one processor. What is the minimum time to complete all the tasks?

options.why: The longest task cannot run at the same time as all the others on just two processors.
Tasks cannot be split in half, so a perfectly even split is not possible.
Correct. Split the tasks between the processors as evenly as possible; the time is the busier processor's total.
That is the sequential time with one processor.

questions.explanation: The best split puts 76 seconds of work on one processor and 67 on the other, so all tasks finish in 76 seconds (speedup 1.88).

questions.stem:

```text
word ← "abstract"
other ← "algorithm"
DISPLAY (concat(substring(word, 4, 2), substring(other, 8, 2)))
```

options.why: The first character is at position 1, not 0.
concat joins its arguments in the order given.
length is 2, so 2 characters are taken.
Correct. Positions start at 1 in AP pseudocode.

questions.explanation: substring("abstract", 4, 2) is "tr" and substring("algorithm", 8, 2) is "hm", so the result is "trhm".

questions.stem:
A robot is on a 6-by-6 grid of squares. Rows are numbered 1 to 6 from top to bottom and columns 1 to 6 from left to right. The robot starts in row 4, column 5, facing right. `MOVE_FORWARD()` moves it one square in the direction it faces; `ROTATE_LEFT()` and `ROTATE_RIGHT()` turn it 90 degrees in place.

```text
REPEAT 2 TIMES
{
   MOVE_FORWARD()
   ROTATE_LEFT()
}
```

Where does the robot end, and which way does it face?

options.why: The robot turns in every pass, including the last.
ROTATE_LEFT turns the robot counterclockwise.
Correct. Trace each move and turn in order.
The robot moves forward in each pass.

questions.explanation: Tracing 2 passes of 1 move then ROTATE_LEFT ends at row 3, column 6, facing left.

questions.stem: A program stores whole numbers using 5 bits, with no sign bit. What is the largest number it can store before an overflow error occurs?

options.why: Each bit doubles the number of values.
All bits are used for the value.
Correct. 5 bits give 32 values, from 0 to 31.
The values start at 0, so the largest is one less than the count.

questions.explanation: With 5 bits there are 2^5 = 32 patterns, representing 0 through 31.

questions.stem: A procedure `countAbove(list)` should return how many values in list are greater than 10, but the programmer suspects it uses ≥ instead of >. Which test input would reveal this error?

options.why: No value equals 10, so both versions agree.
Correct. It contains 10, which ≥ counts but > does not, so the two versions give different results.
Every value is above 10, so both versions return the same count.
No value is 10 or above, so both versions return 0.

questions.explanation: Only an input containing the boundary value 10 makes ≥ and > behave differently.

questions.stem: A data set from a bike-share service contains one row per transaction with these fields: start station, end station, start time, trip length in minutes. Which question can be answered using only this data?

questions.stem:
The following code segment is intended to display the sum of the values in `nums`.

```text
FOR EACH n IN nums
{
   total ← 0
   total ← total + n
}
DISPLAY (total)
```

What is displayed when `nums` is `[12, 19, 5, 5]`, and why?

options.text: 5, because total is reset to 0 on every pass
options.why: Correct. The reset inside the loop discards the earlier values.

options.text: 0, because total is reset after the loop
options.why: The reset happens before the addition in each pass.
total is set back to 0 before each addition.

options.text: 12, because the loop stops after one pass
options.why: FOR EACH visits every element.

questions.explanation: Each pass sets total to 0 and then adds n, so only the last value, 5, remains. Moving `total ← 0` before the loop fixes it.

parts.prompt: (Algorithm development) Explain in detailed steps how the algorithm in `scale` uses sequencing, selection and iteration to produce its result.
